item.title: Sigenergy unveils 401 kWh all-in-one battery for C&I sites
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Sigenergy has introduced a new 401 kWh all-in-one battery unit that can be scaled to more than 4 MWh into Australia as it prepares for a “wave of growth” in the C&I energy storage sector.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese manufacturer Sigenergy has unveiled a 401 kWh battery energy storage system for commercial and industrial (C&I) installations.

The company said the SigenCube fully integrates the power conversion, energy management, and batteries in a single cabinet. The modular architecture has been engineered for high scalability and supports up to 100 units in parallel.

Sigenergy, which has established itself as one of Australia’s most popular residential battery suppliers with more than 120,000 systems already installed here, said the product has been designed to satisfy expected growth in the C&I energy storage sector following the federal government’s recent expansion of the small-scale renewable energy scheme (SRES).

The expansion, that took effect on 1 October, lifted the maximum size of solar systems covered under existing Small-scale Technology Certificate mechanism from 100 kW to 1 MW capacity, increasing demand for both solar panels and storage as C&I companies look to generate and store more of their own power.

Will Hall, Managing Director of Sigenergy in Australia and New Zealand, said the changes dictate that the next wave of growth in storage will be commercial.

“Home batteries have gone mainstream in Australia, and businesses now want the same control over their power costs and reliability,” he said. “SigenCube is our answer for the sites where space, noise and heavy loads have held storage back.”

Sigenstore said the SigneCube is built to meet heavy industrial demands. Each ES401 cabinet holds 401 kWh in a 1,100 mm × 2,450 mm × 1,650 mm footprint, delivering an energy density of more than 220 kWh per square metre. The manufacturer said for a 4 MWh project, SigenCube needs 54.5 m², compared with more than 80 m² for traditional solutions, a saving of more than 30%.

“Businesses are not only asking for more kWh. They want a system that fits on a tight site, runs quietly next to its neighbours and keeps the plant going when the grid does not,” Hall said. “That is what SigenCube is built to do.”

Every cabinet has its own energy management system, and up to 100 units can run in parallel without an external data logger. Operating temperatures range from -30°C to 55°C. Units feature AI-assisted thermal management, active battery balancing, and declared sound level below 60 dB.

Protection runs from the battery pack to the whole system, including a top explosion vent, smoke and heat detection, cabinet-level aerosol suppression, a water firefighting interface and multiple layers of overcurrent protection. Asealed cooling loop gives a 10-year coolant life.

Sigenergy said grid-forming capability delivers 0 ms load-side disruption and MWh-level black start without grid support, with SigenCube capable of 150% overload for 10 seconds.

Units are pre-commissioned at the factory, and basic setup and diagnostics take up to five minutes on site through the app.

SigenCube will be available in Australia for off-grid projects and in New Zealand from January 2027. Grid-connected projects in Australia will follow Clean Energy Council listing.

item.title: Proa launches new platform to optimise renewable energy asset operations
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australian energy technology company Proa Energy has unveiled an integrated software platform designed to simplify and optimise how large-scale solar, wind, battery and hybrid assets are operated.
item.content:encoded:
Proa Energy said its Nexo platform brings the company’s renewable energy solutions together in one operating system that connects plant data, forecasting, bidding, dispatch management, performance analytics, reporting and operational workflows.

The Melbourne-based company said the Nexo platform combines its software and on-site hardware solutions to give asset managers, traders, operational teams and external providers a clearer and more consistent view of performance across assets and portfolios while its modular architecture enables them to select the capabilities relevant to their assets and add new modules as their operational requirements and portfolios evolve.

“Nexo is not an additional layer sitting alongside our existing technology. It is the platform that brings our solutions together,” Proa founder and Chief Executive Officer Victor Depoorter said.

“Nexo represents a major step change. It connects plant data, market intelligence and team workflows within one operating environment. It aims at maximising the effectiveness and predictability of renewable assets, which translates into maximised revenue for stakeholders and owners.”

“Our vision is to power the global transition to clean energy by improving performance, cost and reliability across every asset.”

Proa said 12 renewable energy projects across Australia have already adopted or are onboarding Nexo, representing more than 2 GW of contracted capacity. These include two hybrid projects, with the remaining projects spanning stand-alone large-scale solar, wind and battery assets.

Among the projects are four of Vena Energy’s assets in Queensland and South Australia and Potentia Energy’s Quorn Park hybrid project near Parkes in western New South Wales.

The Quorn Park facility, the first large scale solar-battery hybrid power plant to be built on the National Electricity Market, combines an 80 MW solar farm and a 20 MW / 40 MWh battery behind the same connection point.

Potentia Energy Chief Operations Officer Gabriele Mallarini said the Nexo platform is a key part of maximising the performance of the Quorn Park project.

“Nexo is now part of how we operate the project every day, and we’re excited by its potential to help us unlock the full value of hybrid assets,” he said.

Proa, which recently secured $4.1 million in funding from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency to develop a platform to help solar farm operators detect faults, improve performance, and cut operating costs, said the launch of Nexo marks the company’s evolution from a forecasting and monitoring specialist into an integrated renewable energy intelligence partner.

“Nexo is our latest milestone and the foundation for what comes next. It gives us a platform to integrate new hardware, develop new tools and keep improving how renewable energy assets operate,” Depoorter said.

“The energy transition requires more than building new infrastructure. We also need to get more from every asset: better performance, more predictable operations and greater value from the investment already made.”

item.title: Australian renewable energy investment surges to new heights
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Five renewable energy projects totalling 1.4 GW of new generation capacity and 2.3 GW / 7.1 GWh of battery energy storage capacity came online across Australia in the first six months of 2026 while 12 generation projects totalling 2.6 GW of new capacity reached a final investment decision during the same period.
item.content:encoded:
A new report shows that more renewable generation capacity – led predominantly by solar farms and hybrid solar-and-battery projects – reached financial close, and more large-scale battery energy storage was switched on across Australia in the first half of the year than across all of 2025.

The Clean Energy Council’s (CEC) Bi-annual investment report: Large-scale renewable generation and storage (January-June 2026) also shows that five generation projects totalling 1.4 GW of new capacity and worth more than $2.8 billion (USD 1.97 billion) were commissioned and started operations during the first half of this year.

The CEC said the rolling 12-month quarterly average for newly commissioned capacity has now reached 912 MW, up 56% compared to the same period 12 months ago, and the highest rolling average seen since Q1 2022. A further eight generation projects totalling about 1.9 GW began construction in H1 2026.

In addition to the new generation projects, nine battery energy storage projects worth $4.3 billion and representing 2.3 GW / 7.1 GWh of storage capacity were also switched on in the first six months of the year, surpassing the 2 GW / 5.1 GWh added during 2025.

The report also shows that more new generation capacity reached financial close across Australia in the first half of 2026 than in the whole of 2025 with 12 projects totalling 2.6 GW securing finance, compared with 2.3 GW across all of last year. Utility-scale solar drove the new commitments with 11 of the 12 projects solar or solar hybrids with one onshore wind project also reaching financial close.

A further 13 large-scale battery energy storage projects totalling 1.6 GW / 6.5 GWh also reached financial close in H1 2026, including a record 6.3 GWh in the June quarter.

CEC Chief Executive Officer Jackie Trad said the results show the resilience and growth of the clean energy industry in the face of difficult headwinds.

“Australian sun and wind cannot be cut off by conflict overseas,” she said. “Each new solar, wind and battery investment helps make Australia more energy independent and economically resilient, shielding Australians from global fossil fuel price shocks and supply disruptions.”

The CEC said there are now 141 renewable energy generation and battery energy storage projects worth around $32.5 billion are now funded or under construction across Australia. This includes 76 generation projects totalling 11.7 GW and 79 storage projects, either standalone or hybrid projects, equivalent to 12.6 GW / 35 GWh.  

Solar accounts for 53% of generation capacity at financial close or under construction, and Queensland, New South Wales (NSW) and Western Australia all share approximately 27% of solar capacity either at financial close or under construction,

Queensland holds the largest share of pipeline investment, accounting for $9.6 billion and 4.5 GW in projects that are currently at financial close or are under construction. NSW has the largest battery storage pipeline at 4.3 GW / 11.2 GWh.

“Queensland is leading the nation in clean energy investment, showing what can be achieved when world-class renewable energy resources are matched with investor confidence,” Trad said.

“But the story is bigger than any one state or territory; across Australia, investors are backing the technologies they know will power our economic future and strengthen our energy security.”

Trad did however warn that clean energy investment is not immune to tougher conditions and said confidence appears to be softening, particularly for onshore wind, with investors naming approvals and transmission as their biggest obstacles.

“With $32.5 billion worth of generation and storage projects now under construction or at financial close, maintaining this momentum will require predictable approvals, timely transmission and long-term revenue certainty to help more projects, including onshore wind, progress into operation,” she said.

item.title: Array teams with Australia’s Aeeris to address hail risk for large-scale solar
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: United States-based solar tracker manufacturer Array Technologies has teamed with environmental services company Aeeris to help address hail risk for owners and operators of utility-scale solar assets in Australia.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney-headquartered Aeeris, through its wholly-owned subsidiary Early Warning Network (EWN), announced it has partnered with Array Technologies to expand the automated hail response capabilities of the manufacturer’s SmarTrack software platform in Australia.

EWN’s real-time hail detection and forecasting systems – that combine Australia-wide radar coverage, meteorologist verification, and proprietary detection algorithms to identify hail risks for solar projects – have been integrated into Array’s SmarTrack hail alert response platform.

Array said its SmarTrack software analyses the EWN intelligence and, coupled with automated tracker response, adjusts solar modules to maximum tilt protective angles ahead of severe weather, without the need for human decision-making.

Aeeris Executive Chairman Henrik Thorup said the solution provides Australian solar farm operators with an automated, weather-response defence designed to mitigate one of the sector’s escalating operational risks.

“As solar projects continue to be deployed across Australia, this advancement will better help to protect these valuable energy assets on the grid from the rising risks of damaging hail,” he said. “We look forward to working with Array to ensure that solar power continues to play a valuable role for the Australian power grid through the built-in resilience needed to be protected from hail threats.”

Australia’s large-scale solar sector has scaled from less 350 MW of deployed capacity in 2017 to more than 13 GW by the end of 2025, and much of that build-out sits in regions prone to severe convective storms.

Green transition underwriting business Tokio Marine GX (TMGX) recently identified hail as an escalating risk across that growing footprint.

Francesca Lucia Falcone, Array’s business development director in the Asia Pacific, said as solar expands into hail-prone regions, EWN’s capabilities help Array provide solar farm operators with a clear way of showing insurers and financiers how they actively manage risk and support long-term asset longevity as the sector grows.

“This integration greatly improves the bankability of these projects,” she said, adding that the collaboration complements Array’s existing architecture.

Array said its trackers utilise an AC grid-powered motor and wired communications rather than relying on battery power and wireless communications, that can be disrupted by extreme weather.

“Array’s approach to engineered simplicity combined with EWN’s hail intelligence platform unlocks new potential for Australia that will continuously benefit solar projects by equipping them with tools that make them adaptable when facing hail risks,” Falcone said.

item.title: Virtual power plants explained: what Australian installers need to know
item.dc:creator: Bernadette Geyer
item.description: As Australia’s home battery market evolves, understanding VPP requirements can help installers guide customers toward systems suited to their current needs and potential future participation.
item.content:encoded:
Australia’s growing home battery market is creating new opportunities for installers to discuss virtual power plants (VPPs). Understanding compatibility, customer benefits, and contract conditions can help installers advise on VPP-ready systems as the energy market evolves.

What is a VPP and why does it matter?

A virtual power plant connects distributed energy resources, such as home batteries and rooftop solar, through software. An operator can coordinate these resources to support the electricity grid during periods of high demand.

Australia’s home battery market is expanding rapidly. On 14 August 2026, the Australian Government announced that more than 500,000 batteries had been installed under the Cheaper Home Batteries Program. The country also had 8,846 accredited battery installers.

Under Clean Energy Regulator requirements, eligible grid-connected battery systems must be technically capable of participating in a VPP to qualify for small-scale technology certificates. Actual participation remains optional, although additional upgrades may be required to join a VPP later.

During system design, installers can help customers understand their options by discussing VPP capability from the outset.

What are the potential benefits for customers?

VPP participation can offer financial benefits, depending on the provider, tariff, contract, and frequency of battery dispatch.

According to the ACCC’s June 2026 electricity market report, households with solar and batteries recorded median annual electricity bill reductions of $329–$909 in 2025–26 compared with grid-only households. For VPP participants, reductions reached $762–$1,093.

In New South Wales, eligible households may also access upfront payments through the NSW Government’s VPP incentive.

However, not every VPP suits every household. Installers should help customers compare provider payments, contract terms, battery-access conditions, and backup-power arrangements. The amount of stored energy available for household use may also depend on the agreement.

What should installers look for?

Installers can assess a system’s suitability using four criteria:

VPP compatibility: Confirm that the inverter and battery meet the chosen provider’s technical requirements.

Reliable connectivity: Check internet access and communication requirements for monitoring and remote control.

Scalable storage: Consider current consumption and potential future energy needs.

Local technical support: Assess the availability of commissioning assistance and ongoing troubleshooting.

How Solplanet supports Australian installers

Solplanet is a global smart energy solutions provider, drawing on AISWEI’s power electronics expertise since 2009. Its portfolio includes hybrid inverters, battery storage and smart energy management solutions. Learn more about Solplanet.

The questions and responses in this sponsored interview article were provided by Solplanet.

item.title: 5B pre-fab solar tech gets nod for 1414 Degrees’ Aurora Energy Precinct
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Renewables developer 1414 Degrees has tapped Australian pre-fab solar innovator 5B to supply 70 MW of its pre-assembled Maverick solar units for the first stage of the proposed Aurora Energy Precinct in South Australia.
item.content:encoded:
Modular solar specialist 5B has executed a purchase order with 1414 Degrees to deliver 70 MW of its prefabricated Maverick solar units for the initial stage of the Aurora Energy Precinct project being developed in South Australia’s Upper Spencer Gulf region.

The Aurora project, planned for a 16 km² site near Port Augusta, combines large-scale solar generation potential with battery energy storage and proposed grid connections to supply firmed renewable power to the National Electricity Market (NEM) and behind the meter to data centres and other major energy users.

The initial 70 MW solar PV development forms part of Aurora’s Stage 1 project, alongside an approved 140 MW / 280 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS).

Adelaide-based 1414 Degrees, which was originally founded as a long-duration thermal energy storage (TES) company, said 5B’s technology was selected for its compact layout, which promises to accommodate more solar capacity per hectare, supporting the Aurora project’s potential for about 2 GW of PV capacity.

“The Maverick layout allows us to accommodate considerably more solar capacity within the available land, supporting staged expansion alongside storage, connection infrastructure and customer demand,” 1414 Degrees Executive Chairman Kevin Moriarty said.

The Maverick system is a ground-mounted solar array of up to 90 pre-wired PV panels that are fitted to frames that can be unfolded accordion style. The frames come preassembled on concrete blocks that replace conventional mounting structures, allowing for rapid installation on site. 5B said the solar panels, cabling and connections are factory-assembled and tested before transport to site, which reduces on-site assembly work.

The initial 70 MW deployment will cover 42 hectares within Aurora’s approved 200-hectare solar development footprint. 1414 Degrees said its assessment indicates the Maverick layout could accommodate more than 300 MW of solar PV capacity across that footprint and “supports the indicative precinct-wide potential of approximately 2 GW of solar PV capacity.”

5B said the Maverick units for the Aurora project will be manufactured at the company’s production facility in Adelaide and transported to the precinct for installation.

Moriarty said the execution of the purchase order is a major milestone for the Aurora project.

“Placing this order is a further step towards delivery of Aurora’s initial 70 MW solar development,” he said, adding that the company is now “progressing power purchase agreements, infrastructure partnerships and financing for project delivery.”

1414 Degrees, which assumed full ownership of the Aurora project earlier this year, said it has already secured approval from the Australian Energy Market Operator for connection of the 140 MW / 280 MWh BESS and commercial transmission access negotiations for the proposed 275 kV connection are advancing.

The company is also progressing a proposed 33 kV connection pathway to support earlier data centre development and electric vehicle charging infrastructure.

In July, 1414 Degrees entered into a heads of agreement with an unidentified Australian data centre operator for the proposed development of up to 1 GW of AI data centre infrastructure at Aurora.

item.title: Snowy 2.0 will still be cheaper than relying on batteries for storage
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: The final cost estimate for Snowy 2.0 has been released. The conversion of the original Snowy hydroelectric scheme to a large pumped hydro energy storage scheme will cost $22-25 billion and will be completed in late 2029.
item.content:encoded:
Much media coverage has focused on the major blowouts in cost and time. When the scheme was announced in 2017, then-Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull gave a rough costing of just $2 billion – extremely low for a project this size – and said it could be finished in four years. Engineering issues, stalled tunnelling machines and surging costs of construction all contributed to the blowouts.

The project has endured a remarkable amount of negative press, including from renewable energy advocates. Some of it is warranted – early cost estimates were overly optimistic. Some is debatable, such as claims it won’t work as advertised.

But let’s zoom out. Snowy 2.0 is about 80% done. It will likely be finished within three years. Once up and running, it will convert the original Snowy scheme into a giant rechargeable battery, able to back up solar and wind overnight and during calm and cloudy weather. It will arrive in time to allow ageing coal plants to retire. Once up and running, it will last 150 years. $22 billion sounds like a lot – but it translates to about $5 per Australian per year of operation.

As more and more renewables enter Australia’s power grids, we will need much more energy storage. Building grid-scale batteries with the same energy storage as Snowy 2.0 would cost three times more than the final cost ($22 billion). But batteries last 20 years, while Snowy 2.0 will last for 150 years.

Why do we need so much energy storage?

Renewables currently provide about 50% of the power in the National Electricity Market, Australia’s largest power grid. The government’s target is 82% by 2030 (mostly solar and wind).

Reaching this goal will require much more storage. That’s because over half the demand for electricity is overnight (defined as 4pm to 8am). During these hours, solar output is minimal or nonexistent. Wind provides some power, but not enough.

Coal plants currently meet most of the overnight demand. But Australia’s coal fleet is ageing rapidly and will not be replaced. Almost all will close over the next 10 years.

How can we keep the lights on overnight as coal exits? We can use wind (which is intermittent), gas (expensive and responsible for high emissions), or store energy for use overnight and on cloudy days.

Energy storage has shot to prominence in recent years, driven by rapid falls in battery costs. Home batteries and battery-electric vehicles are surging in popularity for consumers.

In the grid, batteries are muscling in and taking a role once occupied by gas-powered plants to cover short spikes in demand. Because batteries can do this job more cheaply than gas, electricity costs are falling for everyone, not just the owners of batteries.

So why do we need pumped hydro?

Batteries are an increasingly cheap way to store energy short term, meaning minutes to hours. But they’re an expensive way to cover longer periods, such as overnight and during cloudy days.

This is where pumped hydro can help.

Pumped hydro turns a normal hydroelectric plant into a giant water battery. When power prices are low, water is pumped uphill to a high reservoir. When power prices rise, water is run downhill through turbines to produce power. These schemes excel at long-duration storage, as very large volumes of water can be kept in dams and released as needed.

Every year, Australia’s science agency, CSIRO, releases GenCost, an update on changes to the costs for all components of the clean energy transition.

The latest figures show pumped hydro can store and release power much more cheaply than batteries can. The cost advantage is highest now, but it will still be there in 10 and 20 years time. That’s because the steep falls in battery costs are expected to taper off.

Pumped hydro typically lasts five to ten times longer than batteries. Keeping water behind a rocky dam is an extremely cheap and durable way to store energy long term compared to extracting metals to make batteries. Pumped hydro also stimulates the local economy more, compared to imported batteries.

Time to take a longer view

Once up and running, Snowy 2.0 will roughly quadruple Australia’s total rechargeable electricity storage.

Behind the 45-metre high wall of its upper reservoir, Tantangara, is up to 254 gigalitres of water. That’s about 50% of the water in Sydney Harbour (500 GL). This enormous volume of water represents 350 GWh of storage – the equivalent of the energy available in the batteries of seven million electric vehicles.

To stop climate change from worsening, we have to stop burning fossil fuels. To do that, we have to triple or quadruple how much electricity we produce so that we can electrify transport, heating, industry and other sectors.

Almost all of this new electricity will come from solar and wind. We will also need large-scale energy storage so renewable power can be released at night or as needed.

Energy storage is becoming a solved problem. Batteries and pumped hydro can do the job of storing power over shorter and longer periods.

As electrification gathers pace, Australia will need more pumped hydro projects – some as large as Snowy 2.0. The good  news is that the technical issues and tunnelling problems Snowy 2.0 has faced have taught us a great deal about how to overcome them.

The key challenge the engineers of Snowy 2.0 faced is the need for a 27-kilometre-long tunnel. Australia has hundreds of excellent options for off-river pumped hydro sites between Brisbane and Melbourne, located close to transmission lines and away from national parks and rivers. These options require much shorter tunnels compared to Snowy 2.0, meaning they would be much quicker to build.

Snowy 2.0 is no longer a bargain. But it’s still a very good long-term investment.

It’s Australia’s first large hydro project for many decades. Much has been learned, and we now have a highly skilled workforce

Like the Sydney Harbour Bridge , Snowy 2.0 will still be working a century after the controversy over cost blowouts is forgotten.

Author: Andrew Blakers, Professor of Engineering, Australian National University. Andrew receives funding from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA).

item.title: UNSW researchers find east-west ground-mounted PV shows less degradation than single-axis tracking counterparts
item.dc:creator: Emiliano Bellini
item.description: Researchers at the University of New South Wales found that east-west ground-mounted PV systems can experience up to 40% lower rates of certain degradation mechanisms than single-axis trackers. Their simulations showed that lower operating temperatures and reduced UV exposure could improve module reliability, particularly in remote installations.
item.content:encoded:
Aresearch team from the University of New South Wales (UNSW) has compared the performance of east-west ground-mounted PV systems with that of conventional single-axis trackers (SATs), finding that east-west installations can experience up to 40% lower rates of certain degradation mechanisms.

“We investigated how improved thermal modelling can provide more accurate predictions of PV module operating temperatures and associated degradation rates, with a particular focus on the innovative Maverick east-west ground-mounted systems developed by Australian company 5B,” corresponding author Bram Hoex told pv magazine. “Heat transfer coefficients for the east-west system were found to be comparable to those of single-axis trackers, indicating similar cooling characteristics. However, east-west systems operate at lower module temperatures due to reduced plane-of-array irradiance compared with tracking systems.”

The Maverick system is a prefabricated, relocatable ground-mounted PV solution designed for rapid deployment with minimal on-site labour. Each modular unit comprises up to 90 solar panels mounted on frames that unfold in a concertina configuration, with modules tilted at 10 degrees. The system features preconfigured electrical connections, a compact footprint, high power density, and minimal ground penetration requirements, making it suitable for sites with limited usable land or challenging terrain. Its modular design also allows deployment on previously underutilized land, such as mine waste rock dumps. In 2024, the technology was deployed in a 16.9 MW solar installation comprising 342 Maverick units at the Jundee gold mine in Western Australia.

The UNSW researchers explained that the system’s low tilt angles enable greater ground coverage and higher energy density per unit of land, while its prefabricated design simplifies installation. However, accurately predicting the performance of such systems requires improved thermal models, as module temperature affects both electricity output and long-term degradation. Conventional models often overlook factors such as wind direction, mounting configuration, thermal inertia, and radiative heat exchange with the sky. To address these limitations, the researchers developed a transient thermal model incorporating sky radiation and validated it against field measurements.

The team analysed monitoring data collected between September 2022 and June 2023 at a 5B Maverick test site near Bungendore in southern NSW. The installation uses JinkoSolar PV modules rated at 315 W, with module temperatures monitored using thermocouples and local weather conditions recorded by a nearby weather station. The researchers collected irradiance, ambient temperature, wind speed, wind direction, and electrical output data to develop and validate five thermal models of increasing complexity. These incorporated wind-dependent heat transfer, radiative exchange with the sky, and transient temperature effects. The models were calibrated against field measurements, with ERA5 climate data used to improve estimates of longwave radiation.

The researchers then simulated the thermal performance of Maverick and single-axis tracking systems at two Australian locations: Bannerton in Victoria and Clare in Queensland. The simulations used bifacial Longi modules and SMA inverters, with different DC-to-AC ratios for the two mounting configurations. The team assessed two degradation mechanisms: thermal degradation caused by temperature fluctuations and photodegradation associated with ultraviolet exposure, temperature, and humidity. It also mapped expected degradation rates across Australia to investigate the influence of regional climatic conditions.

The analysis showed that incorporating radiative heat exchange with the sky and transient temperature effects significantly improved simulation accuracy, particularly at night and during rapid temperature fluctuations. The improved model was validated against measurements from multiple modules at the Bungendore test site, demonstrating consistent performance across different orientations.

The simulations indicated that Maverick modules generally operate at lower temperatures because their fixed orientation results in lower plane-of-array irradiance. Single-axis trackers receive more sunlight and generate higher energy yields per module, but their greater irradiance exposure also increases operating temperatures.

The researchers found that higher operating temperatures, combined with increased ultraviolet exposure, resulted in greater thermal degradation and photodegradation in tracking systems. Both degradation mechanisms were most pronounced during summer, when temperatures and irradiance levels peaked. Simulations across Australia indicated that Maverick systems were less susceptible to both mechanisms, with particularly pronounced differences in thermal degradation in southern and southwestern regions.

The researchers also noted that inverter clipping and power curtailment could accelerate degradation by increasing module temperatures. They concluded that the lower degradation rates associated with fixed east-west mounting systems could make them particularly attractive for remote installations, where maintenance and replacement costs are higher.

“Our work demonstrates that PV mounting configuration directly influences module reliability, not just energy yield and installation costs,” Hoex said. “It also highlights the importance of accurately modelling module temperature when predicting long-term degradation and lifetime energy production.”

“Our findings also provide a framework for integrating temperature-dependent degradation into PV system simulations, moving beyond conventional fixed annual degradation assumptions,” he added. “Moreover, they suggest that low-tilt east-west configurations could offer additional benefits through reduced degradation, complementing their advantages in land utilisation and deployment costs.”

The findings are presented in the study “Accurate Modeling of Module Temperature for Ground-Mounted PV and Its Impact on Degradation,” published in the IEEE Journal of Photovoltaics.

In previous research, UNSW scientists found that single-axis tracking PV systems experience higher ultraviolet-induced degradation than fixed-tilt installations. The researchers developed a global UV irradiance model showing that trackers can receive up to 1.5 times more UV radiation than fixed-tilt systems in high-irradiance regions, resulting in degradation rates nearly twice as high. The study also highlighted the influence of temperature, humidity, and atmospheric conditions on module degradation, particularly in tropical and desert environments.

item.title: Hoymiles releases 2,000 kWh C&I energy storage solution
item.dc:creator: Lior Kahana
item.description: Chinese manufacturer Hoymiles has launched a C&I battery storage system with capacities ranging from 2 MWh to 2.61 MWh and power outputs of up to 1.25 MW. The containerised system features liquid cooling, integrated fire protection, and backup power switching in less than 20 ms.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese solar and energy storage manufacturer Hoymiles has unveiled a new commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage system with capacities starting at 2 MWh, higher than those typically offered in the segment.

The new HoyUltra 2,000M is available in 15 configurations, with storage capacities ranging from 2 MWh to 2.61 MWh. Rated AC output ranges from 500 kW to 1.25 MW, with configurations supporting AC voltages of 380/400 V, 690 V, and 800 V. The system uses 314 Ah lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells from an undisclosed supplier.

“As C&I energy storage projects become more diverse, customers need solutions that go beyond storage capacity,” said Rex Zhu, general manager of Hoymiles’ Residential and C&I Energy Storage Business. “Electrical conditions, installation requirements, multi-energy integration, backup power, and operating environments all need to be taken into account.”

The system integrates batteries, a power conversion system (PCS), thermal management, a static transfer switch (STS), and fire protection equipment. The STS enables switching to backup power in less than 20 ms to maintain an uninterrupted power supply.

“The system uses liquid cooling for both the PCS and the battery, with an operating temperature range of -30 C to 55 C,” the company said. “It maintains its rated power up to 50 C. It is also equipped with a cabinet-level fire protection system, including smoke and temperature detection, fire suppression, interlocked ventilation and an explosion pressure relief device for the compartment.”

All configurations measure 6,058 mm × 2,591 mm × 2,438 mm and weigh between 22,700 kg and 26,000 kg. The containerised systems feature an IP55 ingress protection rating and C5 corrosion resistance and can operate at altitudes of up to 2,000 metres.

From ESS News

item.title: Lithium demand from storage expected to slow to 5% annual growth
item.dc:creator: Brian Publicover
item.description: Benchmark Mineral Intelligence says it expects lithium demand from stationary energy storage to grow by around 5% a year to 2030, after rising more than 60% a year for the past two years.
item.content:encoded:
Lithium demand from stationary storage is expected to slow sharply after two years of rapid growth, according to new analysis from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, which also estimates the lithium industry will need the equivalent of 134 new mines to meet 2050 demand.

“Lithium demand from stationary storage has grown more than 60% a year for the past two years, but we expect that pace to slow significantly, to around 5% a year to the end of the decade,” said Cameron Perks, product director for lithium at Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

The London-based analyst house forecasts that electric vehicles will account for 76% of global lithium demand by 2050, up from 55% today, “as the rapid recent growth in stationary storage moderates.” Batteries account for 92% of lithium demand in 2026, up from about 70% in 2020, said Benchmark.

Benchmark did not say in its release what is driving the expected slowdown. The forecast concerns lithium demand rather than storage deployment volumes. In January, Benchmark head of research Iola Hughes told ESS News the firm was forecasting more than 450 GWh of new operational storage capacity in 2026, up from about 315 GWh installed in 2025.

Many mines

Benchmark Mineral Intelligence forecasts global lithium demand will reach about 7 million metric tons (MT) of lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) in 2050, up from 2.11 million MT in 2026. At an average mine size of 36,000 MT of LCE, that growth equals the output of 134 new mines, including 44 needed to meet demand growth between 2040 and 2050 alone.

“Meeting 2050 demand requires the equivalent of 134 new lithium mines, more than $100 billion of investment before any contribution from recycling, rising to more than 180 mines in our upside scenario,” Perks said. “The biggest challenge is sustaining that investment through price cycles, while competing for capital with AI, defence and the wider energy transition.”

Benchmark’s upside scenario, with almost 9 million MT of LCE demand, is “driven largely by EV and energy storage policies worldwide.”

Recycling is forecast to account for almost half of lithium supply by 2050. “Recycling will grow, but our base case asks a lot of it,” Perks said. “Every [metric ton] that recycling doesn’t deliver has to come from a mine.”

Benchmark said it expects Australia’s share of mined supply to fall from 29% in 2026 to 20% by 2050, while China’s holds at around 25%. North America’s share is forecast to rise from 1.7% to 13%, and Europe’s from less than 1% to 5.5%.

Storage developers are also beginning to diversify away from lithium. In July, Alfen and CATL agreed to deploy 5 GWh of sodium-ion storage in Europe, with the companies saying the move would diversify materials and reduce exposure to lithium price swings.
